To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the permeability of water and the herbicide benzoic acid was highly correlated across isolated cuticular membrane of Prunus Laurocerasus.
the permeances of 3H2O and 14C-2,4-D were highly correlated over a wide temperature range (15–30 °C).
the cuticle of Prunus laurocerasus is permeable to both water and benzoate, and that this permeability increases with temperature.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of cuticular waxes on cuticular permeability and the effect of temperature on transport-limiting paths of cuticular diffusion.
the effect of temperature on the cuticular paths of water and benzoate transport.
the permeability of cuticular membranes of the European laurel cherry (Prunus lauro-cerasus L.).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

cuticular permeability of benzoic acid is correlated with cuticular permeability to water, whereas cuticular permeability towards 2,4-D is only correlated with cuticular water permeability below 30 °C.
the transport of water and 2‐4‐dichlorophenozyacetic acid through cuticles is governed by different mechanisms.
water and benzoates are co-permeable through the cuticular membrane of P. lauroceras, but 2,4-D is not.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cuticular transport of water is more complex than that of 2, 4-dichloro-phenoxyacetic and benzoic acids, which is due to the existence of different transport paths.

the cuticular barrier of Prunus laurocerasus L. is permeable to water and organic acids and that the permeability to both solutes is correlated at low temperatures, but at temperatures above 30–35 °C, the cuticular barrier is permeable to water but impermeable to 2,4-D, and the cuticular barrier for benzoic acid becomes less permeable.

cuticles of Prunus laurocerasus are permeable for water, benzoic acid, and 2, 4-dichloro-phenoxyacetic at temperatures below 30 °C, whereas above 30 ° C additional paths of diffusion are opened for water and benzonic acid but not for the herbicide.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cuticle permeability is not only a function of the cuticle’s chemical composition but also a function of the temperature.
cuticular transport is not a simple diffusion process, but that the transport-limiting cuticular barrier is a complex matrix with different transport pathways.
cuticular permeability of water and organic acids is affected by the same temperature-dependent changes of the cuticle structure, which are probably due to the melting of the cuticular waxes.
